units.title: Etiopathogenesis of Angina: Stable versus Variant (Prinzmetal)
units.sec: Etiopathogenesis of Angina: Stable versus Variant (Prinzmetal) · p91
units.guide: Stable angina begins with a coronary atherosclerotic plaque that gradually reduces blood supply to the myocardium, so O2 supply falls; physical exertion then raises O2 demand and the imbalance produces the acute attack of ischemic pain. Variant (Prinzmetal) angina has no plaque-dependent supply problem in its core diagram: the coronary artery undergoes acute vasoconstriction (spasm) which acutely drops O2 supply to the myocardium and causes the ischemic pain.

units.title: Management of Angina: Acute Attack and Long-term Prophylaxis
units.sec: Management of Angina: Acute Attack and Long-term Prophylaxis · p91
units.guide: The acute attack of angina is treated with sublingual nitroglycerine as the drug of choice. Its mechanism differs by type: in stable angina it lowers preload on the heart, thereby lowering myocardial O2 demand, whereas in variant angina it acts by coronary vasodilation. For long-term prophylaxis of variant angina, a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) is the drug of choice because it is long-acting and causes less reflex tachycardia; long-acting nitrates, which act as vasodilators, include oral/sustained-release/patch/gel nitroglycerin, isosorbide dinitrate and isosorbide mononitrate.

units.title: Stable Angina: Aims of Therapy (Number of Attacks versus Mortality)
units.sec: Stable Angina: Aims of Therapy (Number of Attacks versus Mortality) · p92
units.guide: Stable angina therapy has two aims. The first is to reduce the number of attacks using calcium channel blockers, long-acting nitrates, beta blockers (best, as negative inotropes), ivabradine, ranolazine, nicorandil, fasudil, trimetazidine, allopurinol and the endothelin antagonist bosentan. The second aim is to reduce mortality due to atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease with statins, aspirin (an anti-aggregant) and ACE inhibitors/ARBs.

units.title: Ivabradine
units.guide: Ivabradine is described as an AHA bradycardiac drug: it blocks the funny (Na+/K+) channels carrying the If current, blocking the SA node to lower heart rate while contraction remains normal. FDA approved for chronic CHF, it is used off-label for stable angina, inappropriate sinus tachycardia and postural tachycardia syndrome. Adverse effects are a higher risk of atrial fibrillation (from increased action of the functional circuit) and visual phenomena from If channel block in the retina - luminous phenomena (multiple coloured halos) and phosphenes (images of light perceived with closed eyes).

units.title: Ranolazine
units.guide: Ranolazine at normal dose blocks late inward sodium (LINA+) channels; at high dose it also blocks the delayed rectifier K+ channel, thereby blocking repolarization. Blocking late inward Na+ reduces intracellular Na+, which reduces Na+/Ca2+ exchanger activity, lowers intracellular Ca2+ in the myocardium and so lowers O2 demand, while BP and heart rate stay normal in a normal person. FDA approved for stable angina, it is used off-label in HOCM and ventricular tachycardia, and its notable effects are a reduced risk of atrial fibrillation and a fall in HbA1c that reverses insulin resistance.

units.title: Other Antianginal Drugs: Nicorandil, Fasudil, Allopurinol, Bosentan and Trimetazidine
units.sec: Other Antianginal Drugs: Nicorandil, Fasudil, Allopurinol, Bosentan and Trimetazidine · p93
units.guide: The remaining antianginals act on distinct targets: nicorandil opens K+ channels and causes vasodilation; fasudil is a Rho-kinase inhibitor that causes vasodilation; allopurinol produces vasodilatation and is also used in gout; bosentan is used in pulmonary hypertension; and trimetazidine blocks partial fatty acid oxidase (pFox), inhibiting metabolism of triglycerides (the main source of ATP in the heart) while promoting glycolysis in the heart, so O2 demand falls.
